item_description: A Norse god associated with light and beloved in stories whose death foreshadows catastrophe.
item_facts: Baldr’s death is told in the Prose Edda and related sources.
Loki is involved in the mistletoe plot in Snorri’s account.
Details vary between medieval texts and modern retellings.
needs_review: Compare source variants; avoid treating Snorri’s version as the only account.

item_description: A monstrous wolf in Norse myth, bound by the gods until the events of Ragnarök.
item_facts: Fenrir is the offspring of Loki in medieval Eddic sources.
The gods bind him with the magical fetter Gleipnir.
Prophecy says Fenrir will kill Odin at Ragnarök.
needs_review: Verify account details against translated Eddic sources and distinguish later interpretations.

item_description: A spelling variant of Freyja, a prominent goddess in Old Norse sources associated with love, magic and battle.
item_facts: Freyja belongs to the Vanir in the Prose Edda’s account.
She is associated with the practice of seiðr in medieval literature.
The spelling 'Freya' is common in modern English but 'Freyja' is closer to Old Norse.
needs_review: Verify transliteration and attributes; source descriptions primarily come from medieval texts.

item_description: A major Norse goddess associated in medieval sources with desire, magic, wealth and the slain.
item_facts: Freyja is associated with the necklace Brísingamen in later accounts.
She receives some of those slain in battle in the Prose Edda.
She is linked with seiðr, a form of magic in Old Norse sources.
needs_review: Details come from limited medieval sources and may reflect later interpretation.

item_description: A Norse god of fertility, prosperity and fair weather, associated with the Vanir.
item_facts: Freyr is the brother of Freyja in the Prose Edda.
He is associated with the boar Gullinbursti.
He appears in stories concerning the royal Yngling dynasty.
needs_review: Verify names and source variants in medieval Norse texts.

item_description: A Norse goddess associated with marriage and foresight, and wife of Odin in medieval sources.
item_facts: Frigg is prominent in the story of Baldr’s death.
She is associated with the household and queenship.
The relationship between Frigg and Freyja is debated and varies across scholarship.
needs_review: Avoid asserting Frigg and Freyja are identical; scholarly interpretations differ.

item_description: A watchful Norse god who guards the bridge Bifröst in medieval mythological sources.
item_facts: Heimdall is said to possess exceptionally keen senses.
He owns the horn Gjallarhorn, which he will sound at Ragnarök.
Heimdall and Loki are fated to fight at Ragnarök in one account.
needs_review: Verify the account against Eddic sources; details are preserved in limited texts.

item_description: A figure who presides over a realm of the dead in Norse mythological sources.
item_facts: Hel is described as a daughter of Loki in the Prose Edda.
Her name is also used for the realm associated with her.
The medieval sources do not map neatly onto modern ideas of a single Norse afterlife.
needs_review: Distinguish person and place; afterlife descriptions vary by source.

item_description: A Norse goddess associated with apples that preserve the gods’ youth in medieval literature.
item_facts: Idunn appears in the Prose Edda story 'The Abduction of Idunn.'
Her apples are connected with the gods’ continued youth.
She is associated with the god Bragi in the Prose Edda.
needs_review: Verify story and relationship details from medieval source texts.

item_description: The Midgard Serpent, a sea-dwelling creature that encircles the world in Norse mythology.
item_facts: Jörmungandr is a child of Loki in the Prose Edda.
Thor encounters the serpent in several myths.
At Ragnarök, Thor and the serpent kill one another in the surviving account.
needs_review: Verify transliteration and myth variants using Eddic sources.

item_description: A complex figure in Norse mythological texts who shifts between assisting and opposing the gods.
item_facts: Loki is involved in the deaths of Baldr and the events leading to Ragnarök.
He is the parent of Fenrir, Jörmungandr and Hel in the Prose Edda.
The medieval sources portray Loki differently and do not define him as a simple trickster god.
needs_review: Interpretation is contested; distinguish medieval sources from modern popular portrayals.

item_description: A Vanir god associated with seafaring, wealth and favorable winds in Norse sources.
item_facts: Njörðr is the father of Freyr and Freyja in the Prose Edda.
He is associated with the sea and prosperity.
His marriage to the jötunn Skaði ends in separation in one account.
needs_review: Verify names and family relationships across medieval text variants.

item_description: A chief Norse god associated with wisdom, poetry, magic, war and the dead.
item_facts: Odin sacrifices an eye for wisdom in Norse literature.
He is accompanied by ravens Huginn and Muninn.
He is fated to be killed by Fenrir at Ragnarök in the Prose Edda.
needs_review: Verify source details and separate medieval narratives from historical religious practice.

item_description: A jötunn associated with winter, mountains and skiing who becomes linked to the Norse gods.
item_facts: Skaði seeks compensation from the gods after her father Þjazi’s death.
She chooses Njörðr as a husband by looking only at the suitors’ feet in one tale.
The couple separate because they prefer different landscapes.
needs_review: Verify narrative details against the Prose Edda; transliterations vary.

item_description: Odin’s eight-legged horse in Norse mythology.
item_facts: Sleipnir is described as the finest of horses in the Prose Edda.
He is born from Loki, who had taken the form of a mare, and the stallion Svaðilfari.
The story appears in the account of the gods’ bargain with a builder.
needs_review: Verify source and name spellings in translated medieval texts.

item_description: A fire-associated jötunn who plays a major role in the destruction described at Ragnarök.
item_facts: Surtr is associated with the realm of fire in the Prose Edda.
The sources describe him wielding a bright or flaming sword.
At Ragnarök, he brings fire over the world in the poem Völuspá and Snorri’s account.
needs_review: Verify translation and differences between poetic and prose accounts.

item_description: A Norse thunder god and protector of gods and humans, known for wielding Mjölnir.
item_facts: Thor is a son of Odin in medieval Norse sources.
He travels in a chariot drawn by goats in the Prose Edda.
He is fated to kill Jörmungandr and then die from its venom at Ragnarök.
needs_review: Verify myth details from Eddic sources and distinguish later adaptations.

item_description: A Norse god associated with law and battle, famous for placing his hand in Fenrir’s mouth.
item_facts: Tyr loses his hand when the gods bind Fenrir.
He is associated with courage and formal conflict in surviving texts.
The Roman weekday name Tuesday derives from the Germanic deity associated with Mars, often identified with Tyr.
needs_review: Etymological identification and attributes require specialist verification.

item_description: Female figures in Norse sources who choose or escort the slain, with roles that vary across literature.
item_facts: The name is commonly translated as 'choosers of the slain.'
Some sources associate valkyries with Odin and the battlefield.
Later literature and popular culture expanded their imagery and roles.
needs_review: Distinguish poetic and prose sources from modern popular portrayals.

item_description: The world tree in Norse cosmology, connecting different realms in medieval mythological sources.
item_facts: Yggdrasil is described as an ash tree in the Prose Edda.
Its roots and branches connect locations associated with gods, humans and other beings.
The number and naming of realms depend on source and later interpretation.
needs_review: Avoid fixed nine-world diagrams as universally attested; verify text details.
